dark pattern|dark patterns: Manipulative UX (User Experience) design (slide 2); considered unfair and deceptive by the FTC in Oct 2021 and by the EU in March 2022. See [Dark patterns can be legal in Canada and still wrong, and act utilitarianism judges each one](#/libs7102-l5/dark-patterns-and-the-law).
PIPEDA: The Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act: it has guidelines for obtaining meaningful consent regarding the collection, use and disclosure of personal information; it's from the 90s (slide 3). See [Dark patterns can be legal in Canada and still wrong, and act utilitarianism judges each one](#/libs7102-l5/dark-patterns-and-the-law).
CASL|Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation: Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation: it prohibits false and misleading statements in electronic messages (slide 3). See [Dark patterns can be legal in Canada and still wrong, and act utilitarianism judges each one](#/libs7102-l5/dark-patterns-and-the-law).
Bill C-27|Bill C-36: Bill C-27's section 16 made consent obtained by false or misleading information or deceptive practices invalid; the bill was dropped on 6 Jan 2025 due to prorogation of Parliament, and Bill C-36 retains this prohibition, under discussion in 2026 (slide 3). See [Dark patterns can be legal in Canada and still wrong, and act utilitarianism judges each one](#/libs7102-l5/dark-patterns-and-the-law).
avuncular ethics: Making something good for a person the default while declining stays clear and possible but hard work, like the pension-plan default; a tiny opt-out box is more paternalistic and violates consent more (slide 4). See [Dark patterns can be legal in Canada and still wrong, and act utilitarianism judges each one](#/libs7102-l5/dark-patterns-and-the-law).
rule utilitarianism: Choose the rule (not action) that maximizes utility; often accused of collapsing into act utilitarianism, since a better rule always adds 'unless in a specific case you can maximize utility through a breach' (slide 9). See [Utilitarianism maximizes total utility, not happiness for the majority or benefits over costs](#/libs7102-l5/how-not-to-describe-utilitarianism).
doctrine of swine: Mill's name for the objection that a life with no higher end than pleasure is *a doctrine worthy only of swine*; it targets the claim that pleasure is the only thing with intrinsic value (slide 12). See [Mill answers three objections: the doctrine of swine, too high for humanity, lack of time](#/libs7102-l5/mills-three-objections).
competent judges: Those *properly acquainted with both* of two pleasures; the one they prefer is the more desirable, higher-quality pleasure (slide 13). See [Mill answers three objections: the doctrine of swine, too high for humanity, lack of time](#/libs7102-l5/mills-three-objections).
too high for humanity: The objection that it is *exacting (demanding) too much to require that people shall always act from the inducement of promoting the general interests of society*; Mill replies that it confuses the rule of action with the motive of it (slides 14–15). See [Mill answers three objections: the doctrine of swine, too high for humanity, lack of time](#/libs7102-l5/mills-three-objections).
lack of time|universal idiocy: The objection that *there is not time, previous to action, for calculating* the effects on the general happiness; Mill replies that any standard works ill if we suppose universal idiocy, and experience shows that lying, corruption and torture are likely to cause pain (slides 17–18). See [Mill answers three objections: the doctrine of swine, too high for humanity, lack of time](#/libs7102-l5/mills-three-objections).
experience machine|Nozick's experience m: Nozick's machine (Anarchy, State and Utopia, 1974) that can give you any experiences you want, is indistinguishable from reality, and you plug into permanently; his three reasons not to plug in show that pleasure is not the only thing with intrinsic value (slides 22–23). See [Nozick's experience machine and Mill's proof put hedonism in doubt](#/libs7102-l5/hedonism-nozick-and-the-proof).
desire-fulfillment theory of welfare|Mil: Mill's *We desire pleasure, therefore it is desirable*: trivially true but circular if 'desirable' means desired, clearly wrong if it means good, since we desire things bad for us, like crack (slide 24). See [Nozick's experience machine and Mill's proof put hedonism in doubt](#/libs7102-l5/hedonism-nozick-and-the-proof).
aggregating utility|aggregation: Adding every affected person's pleasures and pains into one total and choosing the option with the highest total; slide 25 asks *Is it OK to aggregate all utility? Or must we respect the rights of individuals, even at a cost to general happiness?* (slide 25). See [Adding utility lets small pleasures outweigh great harms, and promises bind only when they pay](#/libs7102-l5/aggregation-responsibility-trivial-promises).
strong doctrine of negative responsibili: The utilitarian view that you are as responsible for what you fail to prevent as for what you do; Williams *asks whether we are really responsible for the things we don't do as much as we are responsible for the things that we do* (slide 26). See [Adding utility lets small pleasures outweigh great harms, and promises bind only when they pay](#/libs7102-l5/aggregation-responsibility-trivial-promises).
integrity argument|Williams's integrity: Bernard Williams: *One may have vowed never to kill. Is not killing as blameworthy as killing?*; the blame falls *entirely or at least primarily on Pedro* rather than on the one who refuses *out of moral integrity* (slide 26). See [Adding utility lets small pleasures outweigh great harms, and promises bind only when they pay](#/libs7102-l5/aggregation-responsibility-trivial-promises).
trivial actions: The objection that, since *utility must be maximized*, *we can't take time out. Ever.*: buying new shoes, watching Netflix or going for a walk would be wrong whenever something else yields more utility (slide 27). See [Adding utility lets small pleasures outweigh great harms, and promises bind only when they pay](#/libs7102-l5/aggregation-responsibility-trivial-promises).
promises (utilitarian view): *Promises will rarely be kept, since you only need to keep a promise when it maximizes utility*; breaking one *may cause pain*, but *there's no intrinsic moral obligation to keep promises* (slide 28). See [Adding utility lets small pleasures outweigh great harms, and promises bind only when they pay](#/libs7102-l5/aggregation-responsibility-trivial-promises).
derivative value: Value a thing has only as a means to utility: justice and human rights are not *values in themselves*, so *acting on them will have only derivative value when considering utility* (slide 32). See [Punishment and justice have only derivative value for a utilitarian](#/libs7102-l5/punishment-and-justice).
rehabilitation, deterrence, vengeance: The three ways *punishment produces utility* (slide 31); each licenses an unjust punishment: life in solitary confinement, framing an innocent, punishment that pleases enough people (slide 32). See [Punishment and justice have only derivative value for a utilitarian](#/libs7102-l5/punishment-and-justice).
impartiality: Singer: *We must be impartial (emotional proximity and physical distance do not matter to utilitarianism)* (slide 34); *we cannot discriminate against someone merely because he is far away from us* (slide 35). See [Singer: distance does not matter, and nothing is beyond the call of duty](#/libs7102-l5/singer-impartiality-and-supererogation).
special duties: Duties *to those who rely on us (e.g. our children, partner, friends)*; objection A3 says that because of them *it's actually wrong to be that impartial* (slide 35). See [Singer: distance does not matter, and nothing is beyond the call of duty](#/libs7102-l5/singer-impartiality-and-supererogation).
supererogation|supererogatory action: An action *beyond the call of duty*: *ethical, but not strictly required*, the realm of charity (slides 34, 37). Classical act utilitarianism abolishes the threshold, so *no duty is considered supererogatory* (slide 37). See [Singer: distance does not matter, and nothing is beyond the call of duty](#/libs7102-l5/singer-impartiality-and-supererogation).
threshold of supererogation: The line between duty (*moral - must be done*) and charity (*moral but optional*); Singer's moderate proposal moves it up, utilitarianism proper eliminates it (slide 38). See [Singer: distance does not matter, and nothing is beyond the call of duty](#/libs7102-l5/singer-impartiality-and-supererogation).
strong and moderate versions (Singer)|co: Strong: *prevent bad things from happening unless in doing so we would be sacrificing something of comparable moral significance*, which Singer calls *the correct one*; moderate: unless *we had to sacrifice something morally significant* (slide 36). See [Singer: distance does not matter, and nothing is beyond the call of duty](#/libs7102-l5/singer-impartiality-and-supererogation).
